Liam — appreciate the clear list. Below is a concise, RFP-ready answer. I'm also attaching a short runbook and a topology diagram you can circulate. Happy to redline wording if you need it tightened for procurement.

1) Routing and switchover mechanism:
- Primary routing: we use a combination of regional load balancers + our smart routing control plane. By default traffic is routed to the nearest healthy region via region-aware DNS and global Layer-7 proxies.
- Automated failover: when health checks detect a region outage (based on per-route latency/error thresholds), the control plane triggers a traffic migration policy. For latency-sensitive paths we failover at the proxy layer first (under ~30s), falling back to DNS re-weights if proxies are unreachable.

2) Active/standby model and state synchronization:
- Model artifacts: immutable model binaries are stored in a globally replicated object store and pulled into region nodes on demand; artifact replication ensures model weights are available in target region within minutes if not already present.
- Serving state: request KV caches are treated as ephemeral. Persistent user data and logs are replicated cross-region using asynchronous replication with a write-ahead log (WAL) that yields near-zero RPO for persisted storage.
- Warm standbys: Redwood recommends warm-standby pools for enterprise SLAs — they keep container images/models loaded and maintain warmed KV hot keys for common prefixes. Warm-standby pools reduce cold-start RTO significantly.

3) RTO / RPO targets (configurable by plan):
- API continuity (best-effort auto-failover to proxy layer): typical observed RTO < 30 seconds for regional routing switch. (Target SLO for Dedicated customers: 60s.)
- Full functional recovery (models loaded + caches primed): 3–7 minutes depending on model size and cache priming strategy; with warm standbys this is often < 90s.
- RPO for persisted data (models, training artifacts, logs): near-zero to < 1 minute via cross-region replication and WAL shipping.
- RPO for ephemeral KV caches / session-level token windows: best-effort; unless application-level replication is enabled, expect up to 1–5 minutes of replay/state-loss.

4) Failback sequencing (mechanics & manual/automated steps):
- Automated recovery detection: once the primary region reports healthy and passes stabilization checks, the control plane can be configured to perform an automated gradual traffic shift back (canary ramp) or wait for manual approval.
- Recommended sequence: (a) validate data replication completeness, (b) sync any write fences, (c) warm caches in primary, (d) perform a canary traffic slice, (e) ramp to full traffic.
- Manual intervention: customers can opt for manual cutover at any step (we surface a single-click rollback/cutover in the Console).

5) Observability & verification:
- We provide per-route latency/availability dashboards, cross-region replication lag metrics, and a playbook with health-check predicates used for automated decisions.

6) Tradeoffs and suggestions:
- Warm standbys increase monthly cost but drastically reduce RTO and cache priming time — recommended for high-SLA use cases.
- For lowest RPO, enable synchronous or near-sync replication for critical persisted data; for non-critical ephemeral state, document acceptable loss windows.

Elena — quick technical clarifications below that you can paste into the RFP. Happy to join a short sync if your team prefers.

- PII / telemetry residency: No PII required for routing decisions is stored outside the customer's configured primary region by default. Routing telemetry (health metrics, synthetic check results) is retained in our control-plane telemetry store with a default retention of 90 days; telemetry does not contain customer PII unless customers explicitly enable enhanced request-logging that captures request payloads. We can configure retention or route telemetry to your own logging endpoints for compliance.

- Warm-standby VPC isolation: Yes — for Private and Dedicated customers we support warm-standby pools in customer-managed VPCs or in an isolated project. We can place warm-standby resources in a separate VPC, restrict peering, and enforce stricter IAM and KMS boundaries. For on-prem deployments, warm standbys can be run inside your isolated network and communicated via our control plane over mutually authenticated tunnels.

Additional note on WAL replication: our WAL-based replication for persisted data is asynchronous by default but offers a configurable near-sync mode (synchronous-ack) to drive RPO toward sub-second at the cost of write latency.
